llm-request-response-contract.text: Your service fires an LLM call and gets a 400 back in production. No output, a billing event you can't explain, and a stack trace pointing at the provider SDK. The fix is upstream: a request is a typed contract, and you never learned its required shape. This lesson makes the contract explicit so a bad request dies in your code, not theirs.

Every provider (OpenAI Chat Completions / Responses, Anthropic Messages) shares the same skeleton: you send a model id, an input (a messages array), generation settings, and you read back content, a stop/finish reason, and token usage. Get the skeleton and you can move between providers in an afternoon; miss it and every integration feels like guesswork.

llm-request-response-contract.prompt: Before reading: list the fields you think are REQUIRED to make a minimal Anthropic Messages request, and three fields you must read on the response.
llm-request-response-contract.reveal: Required request fields: model, messages, and max_tokens (Anthropic requires max_tokens; OpenAI does not). Response fields you must read: the content, the stop_reason/finish_reason (did it finish or hit the token cap?), and usage (input/output tokens — this is your bill and your latency).

llm-request-response-contract.intro: A minimal, correct Anthropic-style request and the three response fields that decide what you do next.
steps: model + messages + max_tokens form the minimum valid request; a missing max_tokens is a 400 on Anthropic.
Read content for the text, but never stop there.
stop_reason === "max_tokens" means truncated output — bump max_tokens or continue, do not ship it as final.
usage (input_tokens, output_tokens) is the same object that determines your bill and roughly tracks latency.
llm-request-response-contract.commonMistake: Reading only response.content and ignoring stop_reason — you ship truncated answers as if they were complete, and you never notice because the call "succeeded".

llm-request-response-contract.title: A request is a typed contract, a response is an envelope
llm-request-response-contract.text: Treat an LLM call like any other API boundary. The REQUEST carries four things: the model id, the input (a messages array of {role, content}), generation settings (max_tokens, and — where still supported — temperature), and response handling (stream or not). max_tokens is required on Anthropic and bounds the OUTPUT only; it is not the context window. The RESPONSE is an envelope, not a string: content holds the output, stop_reason/finish_reason tells you WHY generation ended (end_turn/stop = clean, max_tokens/length = truncated, tool_use = it wants a tool, refusal = it declined), and usage reports input/output tokens. Production code validates the request before sending and branches on stop_reason after — because "the call succeeded" and "the answer is complete" are two different facts.

llm-request-response-contract.title: The request/response contract
llm-request-response-contract.subtitle: validate before send, branch on stop_reason after

storyboard.say: Your service treats the LLM call like any API boundary: it starts by building a typed request, not just handing over a raw string.
The request carries four things: a model id, an input messages array, generation settings like max_tokens, and whether you stream.
Validate before you send. If the shape is wrong, reject early inside your service instead of paying for a 400 from the provider.
Only a valid request gets POSTed to the LLM provider, so the contract is enforced at your edge, not theirs.
The provider returns an envelope, not a string: content, a stop_reason, and token usage all ride back together.
Branch on stop_reason. end_turn or stop is clean, so you deliver the result to the caller.
If stop_reason is max_tokens, the output was truncated, so you loop back to continue generation instead of shipping a cut-off answer.
The insight: validate the request before send, read usage for cost, and branch on stop_reason after. That's the portable skeleton.

optionA.label: Validate in your code first
optionA.text: A guard rejects a malformed request locally: no wasted round-trip, a precise error you own, and a testable boundary.

optionB.label: Let the provider 400
optionB.text: Send it and handle the provider error. Less code, but you pay a round-trip, get a generic message, and couple your error handling to their wording.

llm-request-response-contract.guidance: Validate the required-fields contract yourself (A). It is cheap, deterministic, and unit-testable. Still handle provider errors too — but the required shape is knowable before you send, so a bad request should never leave your process.

llm-request-response-contract.question: A Messages API call returns 200 with stop_reason: "max_tokens". What is the correct read?
options: The request failed and should be retried unchanged.
The output is complete; ship it.
The output was truncated at the token cap; treat it as incomplete and raise max_tokens or continue.
The model refused the request.
llm-request-response-contract.explanation: stop_reason "max_tokens" means generation stopped because it hit the output cap, not because the answer finished. The call succeeded (200) but the content is partial — a refusal would surface differently, and retrying unchanged just truncates again.

messages-array-roles.outcome: Build a valid messages array with the right role semantics (system / user / assistant) and know why the order and alternation matter.
messages-array-roles.proof: A conversation builder that rejects an invalid role sequence before it is sent.
messages-array-roles.unlock: You can explain what each role does and why user/assistant must alternate.
messages-array-roles.doNotClaim: Don't claim roles are cosmetic labels — they steer the model, and a bad sequence is a 400 on some providers and silent quality loss on others.

messages-array-roles.text: A teammate "fixed" a flaky prompt by jamming the instructions into a user message and duplicating the last user turn. Quality dropped and one provider started returning 400s. The roles are a protocol, not decoration, and this lesson makes the protocol explicit.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic model a conversation as an ordered array of messages with roles. The system role sets durable instructions/persona; user carries the human turn; assistant carries prior model turns you replay for context. Anthropic takes system as a top-level field, not a message; OpenAI takes it as the first message. Get roles right and multi-turn, tool use, and few-shot all compose cleanly.

messages-array-roles.prompt: Before reading: what breaks if two user messages appear back-to-back with no assistant message between them?
messages-array-roles.reveal: The turn structure is broken: the model expects alternation after the system/first-user turn. Some providers 400; others silently degrade because you have destroyed the conversational structure it was trained on. You almost always want to MERGE consecutive same-role turns instead.

messages-array-roles.intro: A correct multi-turn messages array and what each role is doing.
steps: system sets durable behavior; keep it stable across turns.
user is the human turn; assistant is a PRIOR model turn you replay so the model has memory.
Order matters: system (or top-level), then user/assistant alternating.
To add "memory", you append the previous assistant answer — the API itself is stateless.
messages-array-roles.commonMistake: Putting system-level instructions inside a user message. It works until it competes with the actual user request and the model starts obeying the wrong one — instructions belong in the system role.

messages-array-roles.title: Roles are a protocol that encodes turn-taking
messages-array-roles.text: A messages array is an ordered transcript. Three roles carry meaning: SYSTEM (durable instructions, persona, output format — on Anthropic this is a top-level system field, on OpenAI the first message), USER (the human turn), and ASSISTANT (a previous model turn you replay to give the stateless API memory). The structure the model was trained on is: system first, then user and assistant ALTERNATING. Two user turns in a row is not "more input" — it is a malformed transcript; merge them. The API keeps NO state between calls, so a conversation is just you resending the growing array. This is also the substrate for few-shot (fake prior user/assistant pairs as examples) and tool use (assistant tool_use turns + user tool_result turns) later in the course.

messages-array-roles.title: Roles and turn alternation
messages-array-roles.subtitle: system sets the frame; user/assistant alternate

nodes.label: alternation check
nodes.description: no two same-role in a row

storyboard.say: Every conversation starts with the system role — durable instructions and persona that frame how the model reads the human's first turn.
The user turn carries the human input; the assistant replies. That system-user-assistant order is the exact shape the model was trained on.
Roles must strictly alternate. After the assistant answers, the next message is a new user turn — never two user turns stacked in a row.
You append that new user turn onto the transcript, growing an ordered array of messages that is the whole conversation.
The alternation check is where the teammate's bug lands: duplicating the last user turn makes a malformed transcript — merge them, or a provider returns a 400.
The API keeps no state between calls, so each turn you resend the full array. Roles are the protocol that lets that stateless replay compose cleanly.

messages-array-roles.question: You need the model to follow a strict output format. Put the instruction in the system role or repeat it in every user turn?

optionA.label: System role, once
optionA.text: Durable instruction in system; user turns stay clean. Stable, cheaper (said once), and it does not compete with the actual request.

optionB.label: Repeat in each user turn
optionB.text: Restate the format every turn. More tokens, and the instruction now mixes with the real ask — the model can obey the wrong one.

messages-array-roles.guidance: Put durable behavior in the system role (A). Reserve user turns for the actual request. Repeat-in-user is a smell that the system prompt is being ignored — fix that instead of duplicating.

messages-array-roles.question: Why must you resend the entire growing messages array on every call?
options: To reduce token cost.
Because the API is stateless — it keeps no memory between calls, so history is whatever you resend.
Because the system role expires after one turn.
To force the model to re-read the system prompt.
messages-array-roles.explanation: The chat/messages endpoints are stateless: each call is independent. "Memory" is an illusion you create by replaying the prior user/assistant turns. That is also why long conversations cost more — you resend the whole transcript each time.

tokens-context-window.outcome: Reason in tokens: estimate a request's token load, keep it under the context window, and trim history when it overflows.
tokens-context-window.proof: A budgeter that trims oldest turns (keeping the system prompt) until the request fits a token budget.
tokens-context-window.unlock: You can explain what counts against the context window and what to drop when it overflows.
tokens-context-window.doNotClaim: Don't claim character count equals token count — estimate in tokens and leave headroom for the output.

tokens-context-window.text: A long chat suddenly starts erroring or silently dropping the earliest instructions. The context window filled up and nobody was counting. This lesson makes tokens a number you track, not a surprise you hit.

Models have a fixed context window measured in tokens. BOTH your input (system + full history + current turn) AND the reserved output share that window. A token is roughly 4 characters of English on average — a useful estimate, never exact (the real tokenizer is the ground truth). When input + max_tokens exceeds the window, you must trim, and WHAT you drop is a design decision.

tokens-context-window.prompt: Before reading: a 100k-token model, 90k tokens of history, and you ask for max_tokens: 20k of output. What happens?
tokens-context-window.reveal: It overflows: 90k input + 20k reserved output = 110k > 100k window. You get an error (or the provider truncates input). The window is shared by input AND output — you must budget both. Trim history (keep the system prompt + most recent turns) or lower max_tokens.

tokens-context-window.intro: Estimate tokens, check the budget, and trim oldest turns while protecting the system prompt.
steps: Estimate tokens ~ chars / 4; treat it as an approximation with headroom.
The window is shared: subtract reserved output before budgeting input.
Trim the OLDEST non-system turn first — recency usually matters most.
Never drop the system prompt; it is the durable behavior.
tokens-context-window.commonMistake: Budgeting only the input and forgetting max_tokens of reserved output — you fit the input perfectly and then overflow the instant the model starts generating.

tokens-context-window.title: Input and output share one token window
tokens-context-window.text: A token is the model's unit of text — roughly 4 characters of English, but the only exact count is the provider tokenizer. The context window is a hard ceiling in tokens, and it is SHARED: system prompt + entire history + current user turn (all input) PLUS the max_tokens you reserve for output must together fit. Two consequences. First, long conversations get expensive and eventually overflow, because you resend the whole transcript each turn. Second, when you approach the ceiling you must trim, and the trim policy is a product decision: usually keep the system prompt and the most RECENT turns (recency dominates), optionally summarize the dropped middle. Track an estimated token count as a first-class number in your client; do not wait for a context-length error to discover you were over.

tokens-context-window.title: The shared token window
tokens-context-window.subtitle: input + reserved output must fit one ceiling

storyboard.say: Every model has one fixed ceiling measured in tokens — the context window — and everything you send must fit inside it.
Three streams of input flow in: the system prompt sets the rules, the current turn is the user's new message.
The largest input is history — you resend the entire transcript every turn, so it grows and grows.
Here's the twist: reserved output shares the same ceiling. Your max_tokens is subtracted before the model even replies.
When system plus history plus turn plus reserved output exceeds the window, you overflow and must drop the oldest content.
Trimming shrinks the history — usually keep the system prompt and recent turns, since recency dominates the conversation.
The lesson: track an estimated token count as you go — roughly four characters per token — so the ceiling is a number, not a surprise.

tokens-context-window.question: History overflows the window. Truncate oldest turns, or summarize them?

optionA.label: Truncate oldest
optionA.text: Drop the oldest turns. Simple, cheap, deterministic — but you lose early facts entirely.

optionB.label: Summarize the middle
optionB.text: Replace old turns with a short summary. Preserves gist at the cost of an extra model call and some fidelity.

tokens-context-window.guidance: Start with truncation (A) — most tasks are recency-dominated and it is free. Add summarization (B) only when losing early context measurably hurts, e.g. long agent runs where an early decision still matters. Always keep the system prompt.

tokens-context-window.question: A model has a 128k-token window. Which statement is correct?
options: You can send 128k tokens of input and still get full output.
Only the input counts against the 128k.
Input plus the reserved output tokens together must fit within 128k.
Each message can be up to 128k tokens.
tokens-context-window.explanation: The window is shared by input and output. If you send 120k tokens of input and reserve 20k for output, that is 140k > 128k and it overflows. Budget both sides.

generation-parameters.outcome: Choose generation settings intentionally: temperature vs top_p, max_tokens, stop — and know which are deprecated where.
generation-parameters.proof: A parameter-policy validator that rejects the two classic mistakes: tuning temperature and top_p together, and setting a temperature a modern Anthropic model will reject.
generation-parameters.unlock: You can pick a temperature policy for a task and defend it, and you know max_tokens bounds output not context.
generation-parameters.doNotClaim: Don't claim a single 'best' temperature — it is task-dependent, and on newer Anthropic models temperature is deprecated entirely.

generation-parameters.text: Two teams cannot reproduce each other's eval numbers. The cause: nobody pinned generation settings, and one service set both temperature and top_p, while another set temperature on a model that ignores it. Parameter drift is masquerading as prompt-quality noise. This lesson makes the settings explicit and defensible.

Generation settings control the sampling of each next token. temperature scales randomness; top_p (nucleus sampling) restricts the candidate set to a probability mass. max_tokens bounds output length; stop sequences end generation early. Provider reality matters: OpenAI temperature is 0–2 and you are discouraged from tuning temperature AND top_p together; Anthropic has DEPRECATED temperature/top_p/top_k on models after Claude Opus 4.6 (they accept only temperature 1.0 and 400 on anything else).

generation-parameters.prompt: Before reading: you want deterministic, reproducible extraction output. What do you set, and what do you NOT touch?
generation-parameters.reveal: On OpenAI: set temperature to 0 (most deterministic) and leave top_p at its default — do not tune both. On newer Anthropic models you cannot lower temperature at all (deprecated; only 1.0), so you get determinism through prompt design and structured outputs instead, not sampling settings. Either way: pin the settings and record them with your evals.

generation-parameters.intro: A policy that picks settings per task and refuses the classic mistakes.
steps: Deterministic tasks (extraction, classification) → temperature 0 on OpenAI.
Creative tasks (brainstorm, copy) → higher temperature for diversity.
Never set temperature and top_p together — pick one axis of control.
On modern Anthropic models, do not set temperature at all; control output another way.
generation-parameters.commonMistake: Copying a temperature value across providers. Setting temperature: 0 on a post-Opus-4.6 Anthropic model is a 400 — the parameter is deprecated there and only 1.0 is accepted.

generation-parameters.title: Pick one axis of randomness, and know your provider
generation-parameters.text: Each next token is sampled from a probability distribution, and generation settings shape that sampling. TEMPERATURE scales the distribution: lower is more deterministic/repetitive, higher is more diverse. TOP_P (nucleus sampling) instead keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p. They are two knobs on the SAME thing — tuning both at once makes behavior unpredictable, so pick one (temperature is the usual choice). MAX_TOKENS bounds the OUTPUT length only (not the context window); STOP sequences cut generation when a string appears. The critical provider fact: OpenAI temperature ranges 0–2; Anthropic has DEPRECATED temperature/top_p/top_k for models released after Claude Opus 4.6 — they accept only temperature 1.0 and reject other values with a 400, so on modern Claude you get determinism from prompt design and structured outputs, not from sampling knobs. Pin whatever you use and log it beside your evals so parameter drift never masquerades as prompt-quality change.

storyboard.say: Every request starts with the task type — this is what decides which generation settings you're even allowed to touch.
First stop is a provider check, because the same knob means different things on OpenAI versus modern Anthropic models.
On OpenAI you set temperature, valid from 0 to 2 — lower is deterministic, higher is diverse.
On modern Anthropic models temperature is deprecated, so you skip it and go straight to bounding the output.
The critical guard: temperature and top_p are two knobs on the same thing, so reject setting both at once.
max_tokens caps only the output length, not the context window — set it explicitly so runs don't vary.
Both valid paths converge into one pinned policy — that recorded settings block is what makes evals reproducible.

generation-parameters.question: You need reproducible outputs for an eval on a modern Claude model where temperature is deprecated. How do you get determinism?

optionA.label: Prompt + structured outputs
optionA.text: Constrain the output with a strict json_schema and a precise prompt. Deterministic-enough and provider-portable.

optionB.label: Force a low temperature
optionB.text: Set temperature: 0. On modern Claude this is a 400; on OpenAI it helps but does not guarantee identical text.

generation-parameters.guidance: Use A. Sampling settings are provider-specific and, on modern Anthropic, unavailable — structure and prompt design are the portable way to reduce variance. Reserve temperature tuning for providers that support it, and pin it when you do.

generation-parameters.question: On a Claude model released after Opus 4.6, what happens if you send temperature: 0.2?

It is accepted and lowers randomness.
It is rejected with a 400 — temperature is deprecated and only 1.0 is accepted.
It switches the model to top_p sampling.
generation-parameters.explanation: Anthropic deprecated temperature/top_p/top_k on models after Opus 4.6: only temperature 1.0 is accepted and any other value returns a 400. This is a provider-specific fact you must encode, not assume from OpenAI behavior.

streaming-responses.outcome: Consume a streamed response: parse Server-Sent Events, accumulate deltas into the final text, and read the terminal stop_reason + usage.
streaming-responses.proof: An SSE parser that reconstructs the full message from deltas and reports the stop reason.
streaming-responses.unlock: You can explain the event sequence of a stream and why you still must handle a terminal event.
streaming-responses.doNotClaim: Don't claim streaming is just 'faster' — it changes your control flow: you handle partial state and a separate terminal event.

streaming-responses.text: The product wants tokens to appear as they are generated (perceived latency), but the first streaming implementation drops the last sentence and never records token usage. Streaming is not a flag you flip — it is a different consumption model. This lesson makes the event sequence explicit.

With stream enabled, the provider returns Server-Sent Events instead of one JSON body. OpenAI emits data: lines each carrying a chunk and a terminal signal; Anthropic emits a typed sequence — message_start, content_block_start / _delta / _stop, then message_delta (which carries stop_reason and usage.output_tokens), then message_stop. Either way: you accumulate deltas AND you must read the terminal event, because that is where the stop reason and final token counts live.

streaming-responses.prompt: Before reading: in a stream, where do the final token usage numbers and the stop_reason arrive — in the text deltas or somewhere else?
streaming-responses.reveal: Not in the text deltas. On Anthropic they arrive in the message_delta event (stop_reason + usage.output_tokens) just before message_stop; on OpenAI usage arrives in a final chunk. If you stop reading once the text looks done, you lose the stop_reason and the token counts — so you cannot detect truncation or bill the call.

streaming-responses.intro: Accumulate deltas and capture the terminal metadata in one pass.
steps: Deltas carry partial text — concatenate them in order.
A separate terminal event carries stop_reason and final token usage.
Never stop at "the text looks complete" — read the terminal event.
Truncation (stop_reason max_tokens) is detectable ONLY from that terminal event.
streaming-responses.commonMistake: Rendering deltas and closing the stream when the text stops arriving, before the terminal event — so stop_reason and usage are lost and truncation goes undetected.

streaming-responses.title: Streaming splits one response into deltas plus a terminal event
streaming-responses.text: A non-streamed call gives you one envelope. A streamed call gives you a SEQUENCE: many small delta events carrying pieces of the output, followed by a terminal event carrying the metadata (stop_reason, final usage). The provider transport is Server-Sent Events — text lines beginning with "data: " (OpenAI, terminated by a done signal) or a typed event sequence (Anthropic: message_start → content_block_delta … → message_delta with stop_reason + output_tokens → message_stop). Two engineering consequences. First, you now hold PARTIAL state and must accumulate deltas in order. Second, the facts you need to act on — did it truncate? what did it cost? — live in the terminal event, not the deltas, so your consumer must run to the end. Streaming improves perceived latency (time-to-first-token), not total tokens or total time; treat it as a control-flow change, not a speed switch.

streaming-responses.title: The stream event sequence
streaming-responses.subtitle: deltas accumulate; the terminal event carries the metadata

storyboard.say: With streaming on, the provider opens a Server-Sent Events channel instead of returning one JSON body.

The accumulator hands its assembled text to the client as the final message the user actually reads.
But the facts that matter live only in the terminal event: stop_reason tells you if it truncated, usage tells you what it cost.
The bug is skipping that terminal event: you lose the last sentence and record no token usage. Read the terminal, always.

structured-outputs-json.outcome: Get schema-conformant JSON out of a model with json_schema strict mode, and validate what comes back before you trust it.
structured-outputs-json.proof: A schema validator that rejects a candidate object with a wrong type and an unexpected key.
structured-outputs-json.unlock: You can explain what strict + additionalProperties:false guarantee and what they do not.
structured-outputs-json.doNotClaim: Don't claim structured outputs mean 'no validation needed' — schema conformance is not the same as semantic correctness.

structured-outputs-json.text: A downstream job crashes because the model returned prose around its JSON, or a field that should be a number came back as a string. "Just ask for JSON" is not a contract. This lesson makes the output a validated schema, not a hope.

Both major providers support constrained JSON: OpenAI Structured Outputs (json_schema with strict:true — Responses API text.format, Chat Completions response_format), Anthropic via tool_use with an input_schema. strict + additionalProperties:false + required makes the model emit JSON that conforms to your schema. You still validate on receipt: transport can fail, and conformant JSON can still be semantically wrong.

structured-outputs-json.prompt: Before reading: strict json_schema guarantees the shape of the output. What does it NOT guarantee?
structured-outputs-json.reveal: It guarantees the SHAPE (keys, types, required fields, no extras) — not the CONTENT. The model can return {"age": 999} which is schema-valid and factually absurd, or hit a refusal/length limit instead of producing the object. Structure removes parse errors; it does not remove the need to sanity-check values and handle the no-object case.

structured-outputs-json.intro: A strict schema request and the receipt-side validation you keep anyway.
steps: strict:true + additionalProperties:false + required is the contract that shapes the output.
name identifies the schema; properties define types.
Conformant shape still needs a semantic check (age in a sane range).
Handle the case where the model returns no object (refusal / length).
structured-outputs-json.commonMistake: Trusting strict-mode output blindly and skipping validation — then a schema-valid but nonsensical value (age: 999, empty required string with minLength unset) flows straight into the database.

structured-outputs-json.title: Constrain the shape, then still validate the meaning
structured-outputs-json.text: Structured outputs make the model emit JSON that conforms to a schema you supply. The load-bearing fields: strict:true (enforce the schema exactly), additionalProperties:false (no keys you did not declare), and required (which keys must appear). OpenAI exposes this as json_schema (Responses API text.format, or Chat Completions response_format); Anthropic gets the same effect by declaring a tool with an input_schema and forcing tool_use. What you GAIN is the end of prose-around-JSON and parse errors. What you do NOT get is semantic correctness: strict mode will happily return {"name":"","age":999} if your schema allows it, and the model can still fail to produce an object at all (refusal, hit max_tokens). So the production pattern is two-sided: constrain the request with a tight schema (use minLength/minimum/enum to encode real constraints), AND validate the response on receipt — types, ranges, and the no-object case. Schema conformance is necessary, not sufficient.

structured-outputs-json.title: Structured output: constrain then validate
structured-outputs-json.subtitle: schema shapes the request; validation guards the receipt

storyboard.say: It starts with a contract: a strict JSON schema declares the exact shape the model must return, not a hopeful ask for JSON.
That schema constrains the model — strict, additionalProperties false, and required fields force it to emit only the keys you declared.
The model emits conformant JSON: no prose wrapping, no parse errors, structure guaranteed by the schema.
But conformance is not correctness — you still validate on receipt, checking meaning, because transport can fail and the shape can still lie.
When the receipt passes validation, the data flows safely to downstream use.
When it fails — empty name, absurd age, or a refusal — you reject and loop back to repair or retry against the schema.
The insight: schema shapes the request, validation guards the receipt — output becomes a validated contract, not a hope.

function-tool-calling.unlock: You can trace the tool-use loop: model asks → you validate + run → you return the result → model continues.
function-tool-calling.doNotClaim: Don't claim the model 'runs the tool' — it only REQUESTS a call; your code validates and executes, then feeds the result back.

function-tool-calling.text: A tool-using agent executed a call with a missing argument and threw deep in a third-party API. The model proposed the call; nothing validated it before running. Tool calling is a request the model makes and YOUR code fulfills — with a validation boundary in between. This lesson builds that boundary.

You declare tools with a name + JSON-schema parameters (OpenAI functions / tools, Anthropic tools with input_schema). The model may respond with a tool call (finish_reason tool_calls / stop_reason tool_use) naming a tool and JSON arguments. Your code validates the arguments, executes the real function, and returns the result as a tool/tool_result turn so the model can continue. The model never runs anything — it only asks.

function-tool-calling.prompt: Before reading: the model returns a tool call with arguments. What must your code do BEFORE executing the function?
function-tool-calling.reveal: Validate. The arguments are model-generated text (JSON) — parse them, check they match the tool's schema (required present, types right, values in allowed ranges/enums), and confirm the tool name is one you actually expose. Only then execute. Skipping this runs unvalidated, model-authored input against your systems.

function-tool-calling.intro: The tool-use loop with a validation gate before execution.
steps: Declare tools with a name + input_schema (parameters).
The model RESPONDS with a tool call (name + JSON arguments) — it does not execute.
Validate: tool exists, arguments parse, required present, types/enums valid.
Execute your real function, then return the result as a tool_result turn to continue the loop.
function-tool-calling.commonMistake: JSON.parse(call.arguments) then calling the function directly — no check that the tool exists or that required args are present. Model-authored arguments hit your systems unvalidated.

function-tool-calling.title: Tool calling is a validated request/response loop
function-tool-calling.text: Tools extend the model with actions, but the control stays with you. You DECLARE tools: each has a name and an input_schema (a JSON schema for its arguments). When the model decides it needs one, it does not act — it RETURNS a tool call: the tool name plus arguments as JSON, and a stop/finish reason of tool_use / tool_calls. Your code is the executor: it (1) confirms the tool is one you expose, (2) parses the arguments, (3) VALIDATES them against the input_schema — required keys, types, enums, ranges — and only then (4) runs the real function. You return the result as a tool_result / tool message appended to the transcript, and the model continues with that fact in hand. This is structured outputs applied to actions: the input_schema constrains arguments the way json_schema constrains a response. The validation gate in step 3 is the whole safety story — everything after the model is untrusted, model-authored input.

function-tool-calling.title: The tool-use loop
function-tool-calling.subtitle: model requests; your validated executor fulfills

storyboard.say: It starts with the model. It reaches a point where it needs an action, so it stops and emits a tool call.
The model never runs anything. It only returns a request: the tool name plus JSON arguments, with stop reason tool_use.
That request lands at your code. First step is to parse the raw JSON arguments the model handed you.
Here is the boundary that was missing. You validate the args against the input_schema: required keys, types, enums, ranges.
If the args are invalid, you never touch the real function. You send an error straight back so the model can correct itself.
Only when the args pass do you run your real function. The missing-argument crash never reaches the third-party API.
Your function produces output, which you package as a tool_result turn.
You append that result and the model continues with the fact in hand. The model proposes; your validated executor decides.

conversation-state.outcome: Manage multi-turn state over a stateless API: append turns, merge same-role turns, and trim to a token budget while keeping the system prompt.
conversation-state.proof: A state manager that appends a turn, preserves alternation, and trims to budget — verified by the resulting transcript.
conversation-state.unlock: You can explain why "memory" is a client-side construct and where it is bounded.
conversation-state.doNotClaim: Don't claim the API remembers anything — every turn you resend the whole state, and it is your job to keep that state valid and bounded.

conversation-state.text: A long-running assistant started forgetting its instructions and occasionally 400ing. The state array was being appended to forever with no alternation guard and no budget. State management is a real subsystem, not string concatenation. This lesson builds it.

Because the API is stateless (Lesson: messages & roles), a conversation is a client-owned array you resend every turn. Three jobs fall on you: APPEND new turns correctly (merging consecutive same-role content), keep the transcript VALID (alternation), and keep it BOUNDED (token budget, protecting the system prompt). This lesson composes the roles and token-budget lessons into one reusable state manager.

conversation-state.prompt: Before reading: what three invariants must a conversation-state manager preserve on every append?
conversation-state.reveal: Validity (roles alternate; system stays at the front), boundedness (total tokens stay under the window with output reserved), and durability of instructions (never trim the system prompt). Miss validity → 400s / quality loss; miss boundedness → context overflow; trim the system prompt → the assistant loses its behavior mid-conversation.

conversation-state.intro: One append function that enforces all three invariants.
steps: Merge a new turn into the last one if the roles match (never create two same-role turns).
Otherwise append it.
Trim the oldest non-system turn until the budget is met.
The system prompt is never trimmed — it carries durable behavior.
conversation-state.commonMistake: Appending forever with no budget. The array grows until a context-length error, and every turn costs more because you resend the whole thing.

conversation-state.title: State is a bounded, valid transcript you own
conversation-state.text: A stateless API turns conversation memory into a data-structure problem you own. The state is the messages array, and every turn you (a) add the new content, (b) keep the array VALID, and (c) keep it BOUNDED. Adding means merge-or-append: if the new turn has the same role as the last, merge the content (two user turns in a row is malformed); otherwise push. Valid means the system prompt stays at the front and user/assistant alternate. Bounded means the estimated token total stays under the window minus reserved output — and when it does not, you trim the OLDEST non-system turn (recency dominates), never the system prompt. This one small manager is what stands between a demo that works for three turns and an assistant that holds a long conversation without forgetting its instructions or overflowing. It is also where summarization or retrieval would plug in later, when simple truncation loses too much.

storyboard.say: The API is stateless, so every turn starts here: a new turn arrives from the client, ready to fold into the conversation you own.
First job: add it correctly. If the new turn matches the last role, merge the content; otherwise append, then write into the state array.
The state array is the whole transcript — system prompt pinned at the front, user and assistant alternating. That's what keeps it valid.
Now the guardrail: measure the estimated tokens and ask whether the array is over the window minus reserved output.
If it's over budget, trim the oldest non-system turn — recency dominates, and the system prompt is never dropped.
The trim shrinks the array and loops back to state, so we re-measure until we finally fit under budget.
Once it fits, resend the full state as the next request — this tiny manager is all that stands between a working demo and a forgetful 400.

errors-status-codes.doNotClaim: Don't claim 'retry on failure' — retrying a 400 or 401 just wastes calls; only some families are retryable.

errors-status-codes.text: A flaky integration wraps every provider error in a blanket retry. It hammers the API on a malformed request (400) and on a bad key (401), burning quota and latency while never succeeding. Errors are not one thing — they are families with different owners. This lesson builds the triage.

Providers use HTTP status families with typed errors. Anthropic: 400 invalid_request_error, 401 authentication_error, 403 permission_error, 404 not_found_error, 413 request_too_large, 429 rate_limit_error, 500 api_error, 529 overloaded_error. OpenAI mirrors this (400/401/403/404/422/429/5xx). The dividing line for automation: 429 and 5xx are TRANSIENT (retry with backoff); 4xx-request errors are PERMANENT until you change the request or credentials (do not retry).

errors-status-codes.prompt: Before reading: which of 400, 401, 429, 500, 529 should your client retry, and which should it never retry?
errors-status-codes.reveal: Retry (with backoff): 429 rate_limit, 500 api_error, 529 overloaded — these are transient, the same request may succeed later. Never retry unchanged: 400 invalid_request (fix the request), 401 authentication (fix the key), 403 permission. Retrying those is guaranteed to fail again and wastes quota.

errors-status-codes.intro: A triage function that assigns each status the correct action and owner.
steps: 2xx → ok.
429 and 5xx (including Anthropic 529 overloaded) → retry with backoff.
400/422/413 → fix the request; retrying is pointless.
401/403 → fix the key/permission; retrying is pointless.
errors-status-codes.commonMistake: A single catch-all "retry on any error". It turns a permanent 400/401 into an infinite, quota-burning loop that never succeeds and masks the real bug.

errors-status-codes.title: Status families decide retryability
errors-status-codes.text: Every LLM API failure carries an HTTP status and a typed error, and the status FAMILY tells you whether a retry can ever help. TRANSIENT failures — 429 rate_limit_error and 5xx server errors (Anthropic surfaces overload specifically as 529 overloaded_error) — mean "the same request might work later," so you retry with backoff (and honor Retry-After on 429). PERMANENT-until-changed failures — 400 invalid_request_error, 413 request_too_large, 422 unprocessable — mean the REQUEST is wrong; retrying it unchanged fails identically, so you fix the request. AUTH failures — 401 authentication_error, 403 permission_error — mean the CREDENTIALS are wrong; you fix the key, not the loop. The engineering payoff is a single triage function that maps status → {retry | fix_request | fix_auth}, so your retry logic never hammers a permanent error and your alerts route to the right owner (SRE for 5xx spikes, the caller for 400s, ops for 401s).

storyboard.say: An API error arrives — but treating every failure the same way is why the integration hammers the provider and burns quota.
First step: classify. Read the HTTP status and typed error, then route into the status-family decision.
Transient failures — 429 rate limits and 5xx server errors — mean the same request might work later, so retry with backoff.
Request errors — 400 invalid_request, 413 too_large — mean the request itself is wrong; retrying it unchanged fails identically.
Auth errors — 401 authentication, 403 permission — mean the credentials are wrong; fix the key, not the retry loop.
The insight: only the transient branch loops back. Request and auth errors need a human or config fix — retrying them is pure waste.

retries-backoff-idempotency.outcome: Retry transient failures safely: exponential backoff with jitter, honoring Retry-After, capped attempts, and idempotency so retries do not double-charge work.
retries-backoff-idempotency.proof: A backoff scheduler that produces jittered exponential delays and honors a server Retry-After.
retries-backoff-idempotency.unlock: You can explain why jitter matters and how idempotency makes a retry safe.
retries-backoff-idempotency.doNotClaim: Don't claim a retry is free — without jitter it causes thundering herds, and without idempotency it can duplicate side effects.

retries-backoff-idempotency.text: After a provider blip, every client retried at the same instant and knocked the service down again — a thundering herd. Worse, a retried request that had actually succeeded caused a double action downstream. Retries need jitter and idempotency, not just a loop. This lesson builds both.

When triage says "retryable" (429/5xx), you retry with EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF (delay doubles each attempt) plus JITTER (randomize within the delay) so many clients do not retry in lockstep. You honor a server Retry-After when present, CAP the number of attempts, and — critically — make the operation IDEMPOTENT (a retry of a request that already succeeded has no extra effect), typically via an idempotency key.

retries-backoff-idempotency.prompt: Before reading: two failure modes of naive retries — one about timing, one about side effects. Name them and their fixes.
retries-backoff-idempotency.reveal: Timing: synchronized retries create a thundering herd → fix with jitter (randomize each delay). Side effects: a request that succeeded but whose response was lost gets retried and runs twice → fix with idempotency (an idempotency key so the server dedupes, or a naturally idempotent operation). Backoff without jitter and retries without idempotency are both bugs.

retries-backoff-idempotency.intro: A backoff scheduler with exponential growth, jitter, a cap, and Retry-After.
steps: Exponential: the ceiling doubles each attempt (base, 2·base, 4·base…) up to a cap.
Full jitter: pick a random delay in [0, ceiling) so clients desynchronize.
Retry-After overrides your computed delay when the server sends it.
Reuse ONE idempotency key across all retries of the same logical request so it runs at most once.
retries-backoff-idempotency.commonMistake: Exponential backoff with NO jitter. Every client backs off by the same 1s, 2s, 4s and retries in perfect lockstep — the thundering herd just arrives on a schedule.

retries-backoff-idempotency.title: Backoff spreads load; idempotency makes retries safe
retries-backoff-idempotency.text: A retry has two failure modes and two fixes. TIMING: if every client retries after the same delay, the retries synchronize into a thundering herd that re-overloads the service. The fix is exponential backoff (the delay ceiling doubles each attempt, capped) plus JITTER — you pick a random delay within the ceiling ("full jitter") so clients spread out. When the server sends a Retry-After, honor it instead of your computed delay. SIDE EFFECTS: a request can succeed on the server while its response is lost (network drop), so your retry runs the operation a SECOND time. The fix is idempotency: attach a stable idempotency key and reuse it across all retries of the same logical request, so the server recognizes the duplicate and does the work at most once. Cap the attempt count so a truly-down dependency fails fast instead of retrying forever. Backoff + jitter + capped attempts + idempotency is the whole resilient-retry recipe.

storyboard.say: A client makes an attempt and gets a response back from the service.
First we triage: was it a transient failure like a 429 or 5xx, or did it actually succeed?
On success we finish and emit the result exactly once — no retry, no double action.
If it's retryable, we don't retry instantly — we compute an exponential backoff and add jitter.
Jitter randomizes each client's wait so retries spread out instead of hammering the service in lockstep.
We only loop back if attempts are still under the cap; otherwise we stop and give up gracefully.
Every retry reuses the same idempotency key, so the server dedups a request that already ran.
The lesson: jitter fixes the thundering herd, and idempotency keys fix duplicate side effects.

retries-backoff-idempotency.title: Schedule jittered backoff delays
retries-backoff-idempotency.summary: Implement and test the deterministic decision core for this LLM API boundary before connecting a live provider. const delay = Math.floor(Math.random() * ceiling);  // spread clients across [0, ceiling)

retries-backoff-idempotency.question: For an operation with side effects, is exponential backoff enough to make retries safe?

optionA.label: Backoff + idempotency key
optionA.text: Backoff fixes timing; an idempotency key fixes duplication. Together a lost-response retry is safe — the server does the work once.

optionB.label: Backoff alone
optionB.text: Just retry with delays. Timing is handled, but a request that succeeded-then-lost-its-response runs twice.

retries-backoff-idempotency.guidance: Backoff alone is not enough for side-effecting calls (A). Backoff solves the herd; idempotency solves double-execution. Read-only calls can skip idempotency, but anything that charges, writes, or triggers work needs a stable key across retries.

retries-backoff-idempotency.question: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
options: To make delays longer.
To desynchronize clients so their retries spread out instead of arriving in a synchronized wave.
To honor the Retry-After header.
To guarantee idempotency.
retries-backoff-idempotency.explanation: Pure exponential backoff makes all clients wait the SAME 1s/2s/4s and retry simultaneously — a scheduled thundering herd. Jitter randomizes each delay within the ceiling so load spreads. Idempotency is a separate concern (safe duplication).

items: Delays grow exponentially, capped, with jitter.
A server Retry-After overrides your computed delay.
Side-effecting requests carry a stable idempotency key across retries; attempts are capped.

rate-limits-concurrency.doNotClaim: Don't claim 'handle 429s' is a rate-limit strategy — reacting to 429s is the fallback; the strategy is not exceeding the limit.

rate-limits-concurrency.text: A batch job fired 500 concurrent requests and got a wall of 429s; the "fix" was to retry them, which produced more 429s. You cannot retry your way under a rate limit — you have to not exceed it. This lesson builds the client-side limiter.

Providers enforce rate limits per minute on BOTH requests (RPM) and tokens (input TPM / output TPM), returning 429 with rate-limit headers and often a Retry-After. Reacting to 429s with backoff is the fallback. The strategy is proactive: bound your concurrency and pace your requests with a client-side limiter (token bucket or sliding window) so you stay under the ceiling by construction.

rate-limits-concurrency.prompt: Before reading: you are under the requests-per-minute limit but still getting 429s. What other limit are you likely hitting?
rate-limits-concurrency.reveal: The TOKENS-per-minute limit. RPM caps how many calls; TPM caps how many tokens (input and/or output) per minute. A few large-context requests can blow the TPM ceiling while nowhere near the RPM ceiling. You must budget both — count tokens, not just requests.

rate-limits-concurrency.intro: A sliding-window limiter that admits up to N requests per window.
steps: Keep timestamps of admitted requests within the window.
Evict timestamps older than windowMs before each decision.
Admit if the window holds fewer than max; otherwise throttle.
For TPM, run the same idea on a token counter, not a request counter.
rate-limits-concurrency.commonMistake: Limiting only request count and ignoring tokens. One big-context request can exceed the TPM limit while you are far under the RPM limit, so you 429 despite "obeying the rate limit".

rate-limits-concurrency.title: Pace proactively; there are two ceilings
rate-limits-concurrency.text: Rate limits are enforced per minute along TWO axes: REQUESTS per minute (RPM) and TOKENS per minute (TPM, often split into input and output). Hitting either returns a 429 with rate-limit headers and usually a Retry-After. The naive approach — fire everything, retry the 429s — cannot work, because the retries themselves count against the limit; you just convert a burst into a sustained overload. The correct approach is PROACTIVE pacing with a client-side limiter. A token-bucket or sliding-window limiter admits requests only up to the ceiling and makes the rest wait, so you stay under the limit by construction. Bound CONCURRENCY too (a small worker pool), because unbounded parallelism blows RPM instantly. And budget the token axis, not just the request axis — count the tokens each request will spend against a TPM window. Reacting to 429s (backoff + Retry-After) remains the safety net, but the limiter is what keeps you off the ceiling in the first place.

rate-limits-concurrency.title: Client-side rate limiting
rate-limits-concurrency.subtitle: admit under the ceiling; queue the rest

storyboard.say: A batch of work lands in the request queue. Instead of firing all of it at once, every job flows through one gate first.
The sliding-window limiter tracks how many requests fit under the per-minute ceiling before letting anything through.
If we're under the ceiling, the job is admitted to a small pool of bounded workers, capping concurrency by design.
If admitting it would break the ceiling, the limiter tells the job to throttle and wait its turn.
Only paced, bounded traffic reaches the provider, so we stay under both the request and token limits by construction.
If a 429 still slips through, we honor Retry-After and back off — but that's the fallback, not the plan.
The lesson: you can't retry your way under a rate limit. Pace proactively and bound concurrency so you never exceed it.

timeouts-partials.text: A request timed out at the client, the code retried it, and the user got charged for two completions — because the first one actually finished on the server. Timeouts and partial responses are their own failure class, distinct from errors. This lesson makes the outcomes explicit and pairs them with the right action.

Long generations can exceed a client deadline (timeout) or stop early at the token cap (truncation, stop_reason max_tokens). These are different from status errors: a timeout may mean the server still completed the work, and a truncation is a successful 200 with incomplete content. Streaming reduces timeout risk (you get tokens as they arrive) but you still handle a stream that stops without a terminal event.

timeouts-partials.reveal: Not blindly. The server may have completed the request (and billed it) even though your client gave up waiting. A naive retry can double the work and the cost. Safe recovery uses an idempotency key (so the retry dedupes) or a status/continue check — timeouts are exactly why idempotency exists.

A timeout is retried IDEMPOTENTLY (it may have succeeded server-side).
stop_reason max_tokens is a truncation → continue the message, do not retry from scratch.
A stream with no terminal event is an incomplete failure → retry.
timeouts-partials.commonMistake: Treating a truncation (stop_reason max_tokens) the same as a timeout and retrying the whole request — you pay for the full generation again instead of just continuing from where it stopped.

timeouts-partials.title: Timeout, truncation, and clean stop are different outcomes
timeouts-partials.text: Beyond status errors, a call has an OUTCOME you must classify. A TIMEOUT means your client stopped waiting — but the server may have finished and billed the work, so a blind retry can double-charge; you retry IDEMPOTENTLY (reuse a key so it dedupes) or check status. A TRUNCATION is a successful 200 whose stop_reason is max_tokens: the content is incomplete, and the right move is to CONTINUE the message (append and ask for more), not to regenerate from scratch. A CLEAN STOP (end_turn/stop) is complete. A stream that ends with NO terminal event is an incomplete failure to retry. Set explicit deadlines so slow calls do not hang your service; prefer streaming for long generations because partial output arrives before any deadline; and always pair timeout-retries with idempotency. The discipline is: classify the outcome first, then apply the action — timeout→retry-idempotent, truncation→continue, clean→accept, no-terminal→retry.

timeouts-partials.title: Outcome classification and recovery
timeouts-partials.subtitle: timeout vs truncation vs clean stop

storyboard.say: Every call goes out with an explicit deadline, so a slow generation can never hang your service forever.
When the call returns, don't just check for errors — classify the outcome, because timeouts and partials are their own failure class.
If the client timed out, the server may have finished and billed the work, so a blind retry can double-charge.
The fix for a timeout is an idempotent retry — reuse a key so the server dedupes, or just check the original request's status.
A truncation is a successful 200 whose stop_reason is max_tokens: content is incomplete, so continue the message instead of regenerating.
A clean end_turn is the only fully complete result — accept it and move on.
A stream that dies with no terminal event is incomplete, not done — treat it as a failure and retry.
The insight: a call has an outcome, not just a status — set deadlines, prefer streaming, and match each outcome to its own recovery.

token-cost-model.outcome: Compute what an LLM feature costs: input and output tokens priced separately, scaled to real request volume.
token-cost-model.proof: A cost calculator that prices a call from input/output tokens and projects it to volume.
token-cost-model.unlock: You can explain why output tokens usually dominate cost and how prompt size scales the bill.
token-cost-model.doNotClaim: Don't claim a per-call cost is small without multiplying by volume — pennies per call is thousands per day at scale.

token-cost-model.text: A feature shipped, then the bill 20× d the estimate. Nobody had priced it: the prompt was large, output was long, and traffic was higher than the demo. Cost is arithmetic you can do BEFORE you ship. This lesson makes it a number, not a surprise.

Providers price per token, and INPUT and OUTPUT tokens have DIFFERENT prices (output is typically several times more expensive). Your cost per call = input_tokens × input_price + output_tokens × output_price, where prices are quoted per million tokens. The lever most teams miss: because you resend the whole conversation each turn, input grows with history, and output length is the biggest single knob you control.

token-cost-model.prompt: Before reading: input tokens and output tokens are priced the same, true or false? Which one usually dominates the bill?
token-cost-model.reveal: False — output tokens are typically several times more expensive per token than input. Which dominates depends on the shape: a long-generation feature is output-dominated; a huge-context, short-answer feature (RAG over big documents) is input-dominated. You must price BOTH axes with their own rate.

token-cost-model.intro: Cost per call from two priced axes, then scaled to volume.
steps: Price input and output separately, each at its per-million rate.
Output tokens cost more per token — long answers are expensive.
Input grows with conversation history (you resend it each turn).
Multiply by real daily volume — that is where the surprise lives.
token-cost-model.commonMistake: Estimating cost from a single demo call and never multiplying by production volume — $0.05 a call feels free until it is 50k calls a day.

token-cost-model.title: Cost is two priced axes times volume
token-cost-model.text: LLM cost is deterministic arithmetic. Every call spends INPUT tokens (system + full history + current turn) and OUTPUT tokens (the generation), and providers price the two DIFFERENTLY — output is usually several times more expensive per token. So cost_per_call = input_tokens × input_rate + output_tokens × output_rate, with rates quoted per million tokens. Three levers follow. First, OUTPUT LENGTH is the biggest knob you directly control — capping max_tokens and prompting for brevity cuts the expensive axis. Second, INPUT grows with history because you resend the transcript every turn, so trimming and caching (next lesson) attack the input axis. Third, VOLUME is the multiplier that turns a per-call rounding error into a real budget line — always price at production traffic, not at one demo call. Do this arithmetic before shipping and cost becomes a design input, not a month-end shock.

token-cost-model.title: The token cost model
token-cost-model.subtitle: two priced axes, scaled by volume

storyboard.say: Every LLM call spends tokens on two separate axes: input tokens (system + full history + your turn) and output tokens (the generation).
Providers price both axes per million tokens, but output almost always costs several times more per token than input.
Cost per call is just arithmetic: input tokens times input rate, plus output tokens times output rate, summed together.
Output length is the biggest knob you control directly — capping max_tokens and prompting for brevity cuts the expensive axis.
Input quietly grows because you resend the whole transcript each turn, so trimming and caching attack that cheaper-but-swelling axis.
Now multiply cost per call by daily volume — real traffic, not the demo — and volume becomes the amplifier of every earlier choice.
Scale that up and you get the monthly bill. Do this math before shipping and cost is a number you chose, not a surprise.

optionA.text: Lower max_tokens and prompt for brevity. Output is the expensive axis, so this cuts the most per dollar — if the task tolerates shorter answers.

optionB.label: Trim the input prompt

token-cost-model.guidance: Diagnose first: price both axes for YOUR workload. Output-dominated (chat, generation) → attack output (A). Input-dominated (RAG over large docs, long histories) → attack input (B) and add caching. Optimizing the wrong axis wastes effort.

caching-prompt-reuse.outcome: Cut input cost and latency by reusing a stable prompt prefix via prompt caching, and structure prompts so the cache actually hits.
caching-prompt-reuse.proof: A cost comparison showing the savings when a large static prefix is served from cache.
caching-prompt-reuse.unlock: You can explain what makes a prefix cacheable and why cached tokens are billed at a discount.
caching-prompt-reuse.doNotClaim: Don't claim caching helps if the prefix changes every call — the cache only hits on a stable, identical prefix.

caching-prompt-reuse.text: A RAG feature resent the same 10k-token instruction+schema block on every call and paid full input price each time. Prompt caching would have billed that block at a fraction — but only if it is stable and placed first. This lesson makes the cache hit.

Providers support PROMPT CACHING: a stable prompt PREFIX (system instructions, schema, few-shot examples, a long document) is cached after the first call and, on subsequent calls, billed at a large discount (cache reads are much cheaper than fresh input) and served faster. The catch: the cache keys on an EXACT, unchanged prefix — anything that varies must go AFTER the cached portion.

caching-prompt-reuse.prompt: Before reading: you put a timestamp at the TOP of your system prompt, then wonder why prompt caching never saves anything. Why?
caching-prompt-reuse.reveal: Because the cache matches on the prefix, and a changing timestamp at the top makes every prefix unique — zero cache hits. Cacheable content (stable instructions, schema, examples, documents) must come FIRST; anything variable (user turn, timestamp, per-request data) must come after the cached boundary.

caching-prompt-reuse.intro: Cost of a call with and without a cached prefix.
steps: A stable prefix (10k tokens of instructions/schema/docs) is cached after the first call.
On a cache hit, those prefix tokens are billed at the cheap cached-read rate.
Only the fresh, per-request input is billed at full rate.
Place variable content AFTER the cached prefix so the prefix stays identical.
caching-prompt-reuse.commonMistake: Interleaving per-request data into the system prompt (a name, a timestamp, the user question) — it changes the prefix, so the cache never hits and you pay full price forever.

caching-prompt-reuse.title: Cache the stable prefix; vary only the tail
caching-prompt-reuse.text: Prompt caching exploits a simple fact: many requests share a large, IDENTICAL opening — the same system instructions, the same JSON schema, the same few-shot examples, the same reference document. Providers let you cache that PREFIX so that after the first call it is billed at a steep discount (cache reads are a fraction of fresh-input price) and served with lower latency. The requirement is exactness: the cache keys on the prefix bytes, so it hits only when the prefix is UNCHANGED. That dictates prompt STRUCTURE — put everything stable first (instructions → schema → examples → long context), mark the cache boundary, and put everything variable (the user turn, per-request values, timestamps) AFTER it. Done right, an input-dominated workload (big-context RAG, long system prompts reused across users) sees its input cost and time-to-first-token drop sharply. Done wrong — a changing value near the top — and the cache silently never hits and you pay full price. Caching is the primary lever on the input axis, complementing output-length control on the output axis.

caching-prompt-reuse.title: Prompt caching structure
caching-prompt-reuse.subtitle: stable prefix cached; variable tail billed fresh

storyboard.say: A request splits into two parts: a stable prefix of instructions and schema, and a variable tail that changes every call.
Everything stable — system instructions, JSON schema, few-shot examples, long context — goes first, cached up to the boundary.
The variable tail — the user turn, per-request values, timestamps — sits after the boundary and is never cached.
The first call misses the cache, so the provider writes the prefix and bills it at full input price once.
Every later call with the exact same prefix hits the cache: read cheaply at a fraction of the price and served faster.
The catch is exactness — the cache keys on prefix bytes, so any change before the boundary breaks the hit and re-bills fresh.
So structure the prompt for reuse: stable content first, mark the boundary, variable content last — and that 10k block bills cheap.

model-selection-fallbacks.outcome: Choose the cheapest model that meets a task's capability and context needs, and define a fallback chain for when it is unavailable.
model-selection-fallbacks.proof: A selector that picks the right model by capability/context/price and falls back on failure.
model-selection-fallbacks.unlock: You can justify a model choice on capability, context, latency, and price — and name its fallback.
model-selection-fallbacks.doNotClaim: Don't claim one model for everything — matching the model to the task is a primary cost and latency lever.

model-selection-fallbacks.text: A team ran the biggest model for every request "to be safe" and paid 5× more and waited longer than the task needed; when that model had an outage, the whole feature went down with no fallback. Model choice is an engineering decision with a fallback plan. This lesson makes it explicit.

Providers offer a LADDER of models trading capability for price and latency (small/fast/cheap → large/slow/capable). The right choice is the CHEAPEST model that clears the task's bar on capability and context length. And because any single model can be rate-limited or have an outage, production defines a FALLBACK chain — degrade to another model (or provider) rather than failing.

model-selection-fallbacks.prompt: Before reading: when is using the largest, most capable model the wrong choice?
model-selection-fallbacks.reveal: When the task does not need it: classification, extraction, routing, and simple formatting run well on a small fast model at a fraction of the price and latency. Reserve the top model for genuinely hard reasoning. Over-provisioning capability is pure waste — and it concentrates all your risk on one model with no fallback.

model-selection-fallbacks.intro: Pick the cheapest sufficient model; fall back when one is unavailable.
steps: Order the ladder cheapest → most capable.
Pick the FIRST (cheapest) model that meets the capability and context requirement.
On failure/outage, exclude it and re-select — that is the fallback.
Match capability to the task; do not over-provision.
model-selection-fallbacks.commonMistake: Hard-coding the top model everywhere. You overpay on easy tasks and have no path when that model is rate-limited or down.

model-selection-fallbacks.title: Cheapest sufficient model, with a fallback chain
model-selection-fallbacks.text: Providers publish a LADDER of models that trade capability for price and latency. Good selection is an optimization: pick the CHEAPEST model that still clears the task's requirements — enough reasoning capability, enough context window — and no more. Easy, high-volume tasks (classification, extraction, routing) run on the small fast model; reserve the expensive top model for genuinely hard reasoning. This single decision is often the largest cost and latency lever you have. The second half is RESILIENCE: any one model can be rate-limited, deprecated, or briefly down, so production defines a FALLBACK chain — if the chosen model is unavailable, degrade to the next acceptable one (possibly on another provider) rather than failing the request. Encode both as data: a ladder plus a selector that filters by capability, context, and availability. Then model choice is a tunable policy, not a magic constant, and an outage becomes a graceful downgrade instead of an incident.

model-selection-fallbacks.title: Model selection with fallback
model-selection-fallbacks.subtitle: cheapest sufficient, then degrade on failure

storyboard.say: Every request arrives with its own task requirements, and we filter those into the selector before touching a model.
The selector picks the cheapest model that clears the bar; easy, high-volume tasks route to the small, fast model.
Only genuinely hard reasoning earns the large, capable model, the expensive top of the ladder.
We call the chosen model, but any single model can be rate-limited, deprecated, or briefly down.
If it's unavailable, we don't fail the feature; we degrade to the next model in the fallback chain.
The fallback re-enters selection with the dead model excluded, so the flow keeps serving.
Model choice is an engineering decision: pick the cheapest sufficient model, and always plan a fallback.

latency-budgets.unlock: You can explain why output length usually dominates latency and how streaming changes perceived time.
latency-budgets.doNotClaim: Don't claim a model is 'slow' without decomposing latency — output length and throughput usually matter more than the model.

latency-budgets.text: A feature felt sluggish and the team blamed the model. The real driver was a 900-token answer at a fixed tokens-per-second rate — generation time, not the model per se. Latency is a budget you can decompose and engineer. This lesson makes it a number with levers.

LLM latency has two parts: TIME-TO-FIRST-TOKEN (TTFT — how long until generation starts, driven by prompt size, model, and load) and GENERATION TIME (output tokens ÷ throughput in tokens/sec). Total ≈ TTFT + output_tokens / tps. Streaming does not reduce total time but slashes PERCEIVED latency by showing tokens as they arrive. The biggest lever is usually output length.

latency-budgets.prompt: Before reading: a response takes 8 seconds. What are the two components, and which is usually the bigger one for a long answer?
latency-budgets.reveal: TTFT (time until the first token) + generation time (output_tokens ÷ tokens-per-second). For a long answer, generation time dominates: 600 tokens at 80 tok/s is 7.5s regardless of how fast the first token arrived. The primary lever is shortening the output; streaming makes the wait feel shorter but does not change the 8s total.

latency-budgets.intro: Decompose total latency and find the output-length lever.
steps: Total ≈ TTFT + output_tokens / throughput.
Generation time scales with output length — the main lever.
Streaming cuts perceived latency (first token fast) but not total time.
Given a budget, solve for the max output length that fits.
latency-budgets.commonMistake: Blaming "a slow model" for a latency problem that is actually a long-output problem — cutting 900 tokens to 300 helps far more than swapping models.

latency-budgets.title: Latency is TTFT plus generation time
latency-budgets.text: Model latency decomposes into two measurable parts. TIME-TO-FIRST-TOKEN (TTFT) is the delay before any output appears — it grows with prompt size (more to process), model size, and current load. GENERATION TIME is output_tokens ÷ throughput (tokens per second): a 600-token answer at 80 tok/s takes 7.5 seconds no matter how quick the first token was. So total ≈ TTFT + output/tps, and for anything but the shortest answers GENERATION TIME dominates — which makes OUTPUT LENGTH the primary latency lever, the same knob that dominates cost. STREAMING is the other lever, but it is about PERCEPTION: it does not lower the total, it just shows tokens as they arrive so the user is not staring at a blank screen. Other levers: a smaller/faster model raises throughput and lowers TTFT; caching lowers TTFT by skipping prefix processing; trimming the prompt lowers TTFT. Set an explicit latency budget, estimate TTFT + output/tps against it, and if you are over, solve for the output length that fits before you reach for a different model.

latency-budgets.title: Latency decomposition
latency-budgets.subtitle: TTFT + generation time vs the budget

storyboard.say: The feature felt sluggish, so the team blamed the model. But latency isn't a vibe -- it's a budget you can decompose.
It starts with the prompt: the bigger it is, the more the model must read before it can emit a single token.
That delay before any output appears is time-to-first-token -- driven by prompt size, model size, and current load.
Then comes generation time: output tokens divided by throughput. A 600-token answer at 80 per second takes 7.5 seconds, period.
Total latency is just the two added: TTFT plus generation. For anything but tiny answers, generation dominates the sum.
Compare that total against the budget. If you're over, you've overspent your time and need a lever.
The primary lever is output length -- shorten the answer and generation time drops with it. Streaming only fixes perception, not the total.

safety-moderation.outcome: Add a moderation boundary: score input/output against harm categories and enforce an allow/block policy with a threshold.
safety-moderation.proof: A moderation gate that blocks content when any category score crosses the threshold.
safety-moderation.unlock: You can explain where moderation sits in the request path and why thresholds are a product decision.
safety-moderation.doNotClaim: Don't claim the model self-polices — moderation is an explicit boundary you add on input AND output.

safety-moderation.text: A user pasted abusive content and the app echoed a harmful completion straight back — no moderation anywhere in the path. Safety is a boundary you build, with a policy you can defend, not a hope that the model refuses. This lesson builds the gate.

Providers offer MODERATION endpoints that score text across harm CATEGORIES (hate, harassment, violence, self-harm, sexual, etc.) as numbers. You place a moderation check on the INPUT (before you spend a completion on abusive content) and often on the OUTPUT (before you show it). The THRESHOLD that turns a score into allow/block is a product/policy decision, and blocked content needs a graceful, non-leaky response.

safety-moderation.prompt: Before reading: should you moderate the user input, the model output, or both? Why?
safety-moderation.reveal: Both, usually. Input moderation stops you from spending a completion on (and implicitly engaging with) abusive content, and catches prompt-injection-laden input. Output moderation catches a harmful generation before it reaches the user. Which you enforce depends on your risk surface, but relying on neither is how harmful content ships.

safety-moderation.intro: A moderation gate that turns category scores into an allow/block decision.
steps: Score text across harm categories (0..1).
Flag any category whose score crosses the threshold.
Block if anything is flagged; otherwise allow.
The threshold is a policy knob — stricter for younger audiences or higher-risk products.
safety-moderation.commonMistake: Moderating only the output and skipping the input — you still pay for and process abusive prompts, and you miss injection attempts carried in the input.

safety-moderation.title: Moderation is an explicit boundary with a policy threshold
safety-moderation.text: Safety is not something you hope the model does; it is a BOUNDARY you place in the request path. A moderation endpoint scores text across harm CATEGORIES (hate, harassment, violence, self-harm, sexual content, and so on) as numeric confidences. You wrap the model call with a gate: moderate the INPUT before spending a completion (blocking abusive prompts and catching injection-laden input early) and moderate the OUTPUT before returning it (catching a harmful generation). The gate turns scores into a decision with a THRESHOLD — and that threshold is a PRODUCT decision, not a technical default: a kids' app sets it strict, an internal red-team tool sets it loose. Blocked content must get a graceful, non-leaky response (a generic refusal, not the raw scores or the offending text). This boundary composes with prompt-injection defenses (its own topic in the prompt-engineering course): moderation scores harm; injection defense scores intent to subvert instructions. Both are gates you own, not behaviors you assume.

safety-moderation.title: The moderation boundary
safety-moderation.subtitle: gate input and output against a policy threshold

storyboard.say: A user submits input. Before we spend a single completion, that input has to cross a boundary we built on purpose.
The input moderator scores the text across harm categories — hate, harassment, violence, self-harm — turning words into numeric confidences.
If the input clears the policy threshold, it is clean, and only then do we spend a call on the model.
If the input is flagged, we stop early — no completion spent, abusive prompts and injection caught at the door.
The model answers, but its output is not trusted yet — it goes straight into a second moderation gate before anyone sees it.
Clean output is returned to the user; flagged output is refused, catching a harmful generation the model produced on its own.
Both flags land on one graceful block, not an error — and the threshold that decides is a product call: strict for kids, loose for red-teaming.
