llm-observability.outcome: Instrument LLM calls so you can answer: how slow (p50/p95 latency), how often failing (error rate), and how expensive (tokens) — from real logs.
llm-observability.proof: A metrics summarizer that computes p50/p95 latency, error rate, and total tokens from call logs.
llm-observability.unlock: You can explain why p95 matters more than the average and what to log on every call.
llm-observability.doNotClaim: Don't claim a feature is 'fast' from the average latency — the tail (p95/p99) is what users feel and what breaks SLAs.

llm-observability.text: A feature "looked fine" on average but a slice of users hit 10-second waits and silent failures nobody could quantify. Without per-call telemetry, you are flying blind. This lesson makes latency, errors, and cost into measured numbers.

Treat every LLM call like any external dependency: log latency, success/failure, token usage (input/output), model, and stop_reason. From those logs you compute the operational picture — PERCENTILE latency (p50 is typical, p95/p99 is the tail users feel), ERROR RATE by status family, and TOKEN/COST totals. Averages hide the tail; percentiles expose it.

llm-observability.prompt: Before reading: your average latency is 300ms but users complain it is slow. What metric are you missing?
llm-observability.reveal: The tail — p95/p99 latency. A 300ms average can hide a p95 of 4s if a slice of requests (long outputs, cold caches, retries) are much slower. Users experience the tail, not the mean. You also want error rate by family and token/cost per call — none of which the average latency shows.

llm-observability.intro: Summarize call logs into the three operational numbers.
steps: Log latency, ok/fail, and token usage on every call.
p50 is the typical experience; p95/p99 is the tail that hurts.
Error rate is failures over total, ideally split by status family.
Total tokens ties observability back to the cost model.
llm-observability.commonMistake: Reporting only the average latency. It smooths over the slow tail, so an SLA breach affecting 5% of users is invisible until they churn.

llm-observability.title: Percentiles, error rate, and tokens — logged per call
llm-observability.text: You cannot operate what you do not measure, and LLM calls are an external dependency like any other. Log, on EVERY call: latency, success/failure (with status), token usage (input and output), the model, and stop_reason. From that stream you compute three operational views. LATENCY as PERCENTILES: p50 is the median (typical) experience, but p95/p99 is the TAIL — the slow slice that users actually feel and that breaks SLAs; the average hides it, so always report percentiles. ERROR RATE: failures over total, ideally broken down by status family (a 429 spike means rate limits, a 5xx spike means the provider, a 400 spike means your requests). TOKEN/COST: totals and per-call, which connects observability directly to the cost model. This telemetry is also what makes EVALUATION and A/B testing possible — you cannot attribute a quality or cost change to a prompt or model change if you were not recording the per-call facts. Instrument first; optimize second.

storyboard.say: A feature looked fine on average, but a slice of users hit 10-second waits and silent failures nobody could count. Without telemetry, you fly blind.
So treat every LLM call like any external dependency: on each call, emit a log with latency, status, token usage, model, and stop_reason.
From that one log stream you compute three operational views. First, roll the latencies into percentiles.
p50 is the typical experience, but p95 and p99 are the tail users actually feel. The average hides that slow slice, so always report percentiles.
Second, compute error rate as failures over total, broken down by status family: 429 means rate limits, 5xx the provider, 400 your requests.
Third, sum token usage into cost totals and per-call spend, connecting observability directly to the bill.
Percentiles report the latency picture and error rates raise alerts, both landing on the dashboard where the tail becomes visible.
The core insight: you cannot operate what you do not measure. Log every call, and blind averages become numbers you can act on.

optionA.label: Percentiles
optionA.text: p50 for typical, p95/p99 for the tail. Exposes the slow slice that breaks SLAs and drives complaints.

secrets-provider-boundary.outcome: Keep API keys out of code and clients, and hide the provider behind a seam so you can swap or fall back without touching callers.
secrets-provider-boundary.proof: A scanner that flags a hardcoded key and a credential not sourced from the environment.
secrets-provider-boundary.unlock: You can explain why the key must live server-side and how a provider seam enables fallback.
secrets-provider-boundary.doNotClaim: Don't claim a key in a config file is fine — any key in source or shipped to a client is a leaked key.

secrets-provider-boundary.text: An API key was committed in a source file and later shipped in a client bundle; it was scraped and ran up a bill within hours. And because every call hard-referenced one provider's SDK, adding a fallback meant editing dozens of call sites. Secrets and coupling are both production risks. This lesson closes both.

Two production concerns converge here. SECRETS: the API key is a bearer credential — anyone who has it can spend your money — so it must live server-side, loaded from the environment or a secret manager, never hardcoded and never sent to a browser. PROVIDER BOUNDARY: wrapping the provider SDK behind your own small interface (a seam) means model selection, fallbacks, retries, and observability live in one place, and swapping or adding a provider does not ripple through the codebase.

secrets-provider-boundary.prompt: Before reading: two things must never happen to an LLM API key. What are they, and where should the key live?
secrets-provider-boundary.reveal: Never hardcode it in source (it lands in git history and can be scraped), and never ship it to a client/browser (anyone can read the bundle). The key lives server-side, loaded from an environment variable or a secret manager, and all model calls go through your server — the browser calls YOUR backend, which holds the key.

secrets-provider-boundary.intro: A scanner for the two secret mistakes, plus the seam that isolates the provider.
steps: Load the key from the environment (or a secret manager) at the server boundary.
Fail fast at startup if a required secret is missing.
The browser calls your backend; the backend holds the key — never the client.
A single provider seam is where fallback, retries, and logging live.
secrets-provider-boundary.commonMistake: Hardcoding the key "just for now" or exposing it via a client-readable env var (e.g. a NEXT_PUBLIC_/VITE_ prefix). Both ship the secret to anyone who looks — treat prefixed env vars as public.

secrets-provider-boundary.title: Key server-side, provider behind a seam
secrets-provider-boundary.text: Two disciplines make an LLM integration production-safe. SECRETS: an API key is a bearer token — possession is permission — so it must never be hardcoded (it enters version control and can be scraped) and never shipped to a client (browser bundles and public-prefixed env vars are readable by anyone). The key lives on the server, loaded from an environment variable or secret manager, validated at startup so a missing secret fails fast; the browser talks to YOUR backend, which holds the key. THE PROVIDER BOUNDARY: rather than scattering provider-SDK calls across the codebase, wrap the provider behind one small interface — a seam. Everything the course has built (model selection, fallback chains, retries with backoff, moderation, observability) lives BEHIND that seam, so callers depend on your interface, not a vendor. The payoff is swappability: adding a fallback provider or migrating is a change in one place, not a hundred, and you can even A/B two providers behind the same interface. Secrets protect the money; the seam protects your ability to change.

capstone-resilient-streaming-client.text: Every earlier lesson built one primitive: the request contract, SSE parsing, error triage, backoff, cost. Production needs them working TOGETHER on one call path — a transient failure, a clean streamed retry, an accounted cost. This capstone composes them and proves the whole is correct.

A production LLM call is not a single fetch — it is a small state machine. It attempts the call; on a transient error (429/5xx) it computes a jittered/exponential backoff and retries (idempotently); on success it consumes the SSE stream, accumulates deltas, and reads the terminal event for stop_reason and usage; and it tracks cost across the whole thing. This capstone wires the course's primitives into that path and runs a scripted scenario end to end.

capstone-resilient-streaming-client.title: A resilient call is a state machine over the primitives
capstone-resilient-streaming-client.text: Everything the course taught converges into one call path, and the discipline is COMPOSITION. Model the call as a small state machine: ATTEMPT → classify (triage) → on transient failure, BACKOFF and retry (with an idempotency key); on success, STREAM (parse SSE, accumulate deltas) → read the TERMINAL event (stop_reason + usage) → account COST. Each transition is a primitive you already built and tested in isolation; the capstone proves they fit together without dropping a concern — the retry still streams, the stream still reads its terminal event, the cost still accrues across attempts. The output is a RUN REPORT: the final text, the stop_reason, how many retries and what delays, and the total cost. That report is the "proof, not vibes" artifact for the whole course — it shows a real transient failure recovered, a clean streamed result, and an accounted cost, all on one path. Build features this way: not as a lucky single fetch, but as an explicit, observable state machine over primitives you can each defend.

storyboard.say: Every production LLM call starts here: we attempt the request, then read back its status to decide what happens next.
Triage is the decision point. It classifies the response: a transient 429 or 5xx means retry, a clean response means proceed.
On a transient failure we don't just retry blindly: we compute a jittered exponential backoff, then re-attempt with the same idempotency key.
The retry loops back through triage, so the SAME state machine governs the second try; nothing about streaming or cost gets bypassed.
When triage sees a clean response, we hand off to the stream: parse the SSE frames, accumulate deltas, and read the terminal event for stop_reason and usage.
That terminal usage feeds cost accrual, which accumulates across every attempt, so retries never drop a token count.
It all converges into one run report: final text, stop_reason, how many retries and delays, and total cost. That is composition proven end to end.
